extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of classical Roman drama and comedy (general readers interested in Plautus)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the evaluative features, stylistic devices, stagecraft, and character-types typical of Plautus' Roman comedies for literary analysis or emulative composition. Focuses on how themes, language, meter, and performance conditions shape comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political vs domestic content (New Comedy influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek New Comedy is described as 'devoid of a serious political, social or intellectual content' and focused on home and the family; Plautus adapts this but sometimes matches the complex public mood (e.g., subtle antiwar feeling) without explicit political reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a play foregrounds household/domestic situations (safe, widely performable) or whether it encodes political/social commentary subtly (e.g., emphasis on officium, pietas, economic hardship). Note that explicit political risk-taking is characteristic of Old Comedy but largely absent from New Comedy and its Plautine adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of father–son relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Father–son relations are a recurring theme: focus on proper conduct, loyalty, and sometimes betrayal; reflective of a patriarchal society where this relationship is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how central the father–son dynamic is to the plot and moral message, whether it emphasizes duty/pietas, and whether it presents betrayal or idealized loyalty. This theme signals domestic focus and Roman social values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of farce and believability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus' plays are often characterized as farcical and 'much less believable' than Menander's, producing 'incredulity and refusal of sympathy of the audience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the extent of exaggeration, caricature, and improbability. High farce (broad, ludicrous situations) is an expected Plautine trait; lower believability is not necessarily a flaw but a stylistic choice geared to broad humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologue verbosity and function
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautine prologues are noted for their 'verbosity' and function to 'win his audience'; they often supply exposition and a direct address to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prologues for how they orient the audience, provide exposition, and employ persuasive verbosity. Consider whether wordiness serves theatrical necessity (winning attention) and how it balances information with entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wordplay (paronomasia), alliteration, and punning
rubrics_metrics.description: Word play is essential: puns, alliteration, paronomasia, and made-up/shifted word meanings are common, e.g., character names carrying comic meaning (Philocomasium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess density and inventiveness of linguistic humor: name jokes, puns, paronomasia, and playful semantic shifts. This is a core comic device; its effectiveness depends on audience recognition and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on stock characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus frequently uses stock characters (slaves, concubines, soldiers, old men) and repeats character-types when they amuse audiences; 'Everything... were sacrificed to humor'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters function as broad archetypes serving comedic situations rather than psychologically complex individuals. Stock-character utility for plot and humor is a positive Plautine feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: The clever slave (servus callidus) as central comic engine
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'clever slave' provides exposition and humor and often drives the plot; Plautus enlarges this role compared to Greek precedents, using monologue, imperatives, and audience address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at the slave's share of monologue, use of imperatives, ingenuity in plotting, and capacity to elicit audience sympathy despite deceit. The slave's effectiveness is a primary metric of Plautine comic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Greek language and Greek cultural references
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive use of Greek names (approx. 250 of ~270 proper names) and Greek words which likely produced comic effect for an audience with some Greek knowledge; Greek terms often mark foods, trades, or low-status speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the strategic insertion of Greek vocabulary/names to signal foreignness, social status, or to create bilingual jokes. Consider contemporary audience competence in Greek when judging effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contaminatio (mixing of source plays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus frequently practices 'contaminatio', mixing elements of two or more source plays to create a new plot; e.g., adding tricks beyond the Greek original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating originality/adaptation, note how Plautus blends, cuts, exaggerates, or reorders source-material elements. Contaminatio is an adaptive method rather than plagiarism and often increases comic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stagecraft adapted to temporary, small wooden stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman stages were shallow and long, temporary, with three openings; lack of permanent theater and orchestra shaped limited movement and an acting style relying more on voice and proximity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze blocking, entrances/exits, and emphasis on vocal delivery and proximate audience engagement. Expect restrained physicality but heightened vocal and rhetorical strategies suited to intimate staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festival (ludi) performance context
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautine drama was performed during ludi (religious festival games) on temporary stages near temples; seating and visibility were socially determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how religious festival context and audience composition (statused seating, standing lower classes) influence content, spectacle, and acceptable levels of social inversion or ribaldry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography of the stage and spatial semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage geography often mirrored city geography so audiences were oriented to locale; exits/entrances and specific offstage locations signal social standing and thematic contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how spatial arrangements encode social position or thematic opposition (male/outside vs female/inside), and how verbs of motion in dialogue function as stage directions. Consider use of 'cover monologue' to mark time transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct relationship with the audience (proximity and address)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small stages fostered close actor–audience interaction; actors often spoke directly to the audience and sought their attention and acknowledgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess techniques of direct address (prologues, asides, soliloquies) and how they cultivate immediacy, audience complicity, or topical rapport. Proximity-driven styles (imperative, monologue) are central to comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency subordinated to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization and consistency could be 'sacrificed to humor'; persona stays where necessary for plot and humor rather than full psychological realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge characters by their service to comedy and plot rather than by realist consistency. Recurring archetypal behavior is an acceptable and expected technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senex amator (lustful old man) as a stock figure
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'senex amator' (lustful old man) is ridiculed: motivations shown as animal passion, childish behavior, reverting to youthful love-language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portrayals for comic ridicule, imagery of animal passion, and how the figure's attempts create humorous situations. This archetype commonly produces mockery and inversion of dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female role designations and social signaling
rubrics_metrics.description: Female role labels (mulier, virgo, ancilla, anus, meretrix, lena) are used variably to indicate social status and marital condition; designations can shift in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how role-terms signal rank, sexual status, or social function, and how fluctuations in designation affect interpretation of female characters and their agency within the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming (and unnamed characters) as indicator of importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 18% of characters are unnamed; important characters usually have names while minor ones may not, though there are exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence of names in scene headings/text as a heuristic for character prominence, but watch exceptions where a main character may remain unnamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colloquial Latin style and archaic irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus writes in a colloquial, non-classical Latin full of irregularities and archaic forms (e.g., mavolo, dic(e), retention of -u- vs -i-, prodelision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate register and dialectal/chronological features as deliberate stylistic choices reproducing everyday speech. Irregular forms often occur in promises, threats, prologues, and speeches and are metrically convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proverbs and foreign-language passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus uses proverbs widely (often at the end of soliloquies) and sometimes inserts passages in other languages (Greek, Punic) for authenticity or character effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proverbs for thematic emphasis or comic punctuation; judge foreign-language passages for their contribution to authenticity, characterisation, or obliquely comic exoticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic/sound devices (alliteration, assonance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus uses technical devices such as alliteration and assonance to express character traits and assert authority (e.g., Palaestrio's strings of similar-sounding words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze sound-patterning as a rhetorical tool for humor, character voice, or emphasis. Dense alliteration can signal cleverness, bravado, or verbal showmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes and riddle-type wordplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Riddle jokes and 'knock knock - who's there?' patterns, inventing and changing word meanings, and other verbal joke forms are abundant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess structural joke types (riddle, pun, invented-word gag) and their placement. Consider audience literacy in references and word-forms when judging comic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter and rhythmic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Plautus uses varied meters, most frequently the iambic senarius and the trochaic septenarius, and often favors cantica over Greek meters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how metrical choice shapes delivery, musicality, and mood; changes of meter (e.g., from senarii to iambic septenarii) often signal shifts in tone or time and can be used to distract or reorient the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigor, immediacy, and use of monologue/imperative mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves account for large amounts of monologue used for humor, moralizing, exposition; the imperative mood effects 'forceful inversion' (master reduced to supplicant) and contributes to role reversal and exaltation of humble characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the effectiveness of monologues and imperative speech in creating immediacy, inverting social hierarchies, and climaxing comic reversal. These devices are central to Plautine finale mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural detail and everyday material (e.g., food references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent references to everyday items (meat, especially pork) and local Roman locales that orient the audience and add realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate use of quotidian detail as a means to ground comedy in Roman life and to produce local, material humor that resonates with the audience.
